concepts.label: What Is a Resource?
concepts.cardText: Everything available in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable, can be termed a resource. Turning things in the environment into resources involves an interactive relationship between nature, technology and institutions. Resources are not free gifts of nature: they are a function of human activities, and human beings themselves are essential components of resources.

concepts.label: Problems of Indiscriminate Use of Resources
concepts.cardText: Resources are vital for human survival and for the quality of life. Because people believed resources were free gifts of nature, they used them indiscriminately. This has led to depletion of resources for satisfying the greed of a few individuals; accumulation of resources in few hands, dividing society into haves and have nots, rich and poor; and global ecological crises such as global warming, ozone layer depletion, environmental pollution and land degradation.

concepts.label: Sustainable Development and the Rio Earth Summit
concepts.cardText: Sustainable economic development means development should take place without damaging the environment, and development in the present should not compromise with the needs of future generations. In June 1992, more than 100 heads of states met at the first International Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. They signed the Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity, endorsed the global Forest Principles and adopted Agenda 21 for sustainable development in the 21st century. Agenda 21 aims to combat environmental damage, poverty and disease through global co-operation; every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21. An equitable distribution of resources is essential, so resource planning is essential for sustainable existence.

concepts.label: Need for Balanced Resource Planning
concepts.cardText: Planning is the widely accepted strategy for judicious use of resources, and it is important in India because of its enormous diversity in resources. Some regions are rich in some resources but deficient in others: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh are rich in minerals and coal; Arunachal Pradesh has abundant water but lacks infrastructure; Rajasthan is endowed with solar and wind energy but lacks water; the cold desert of Ladakh has rich cultural heritage but is deficient in water, infrastructure and some vital minerals. This calls for balanced resource planning at the national, state, regional and local levels.

concepts.label: Resource Planning in India
concepts.cardText: Resource planning in India involves three steps: (i) identifying and making an inventory of resources across regions, by surveying, mapping and estimating them; (ii) evolving a planning structure with appropriate technology, skill and institutional set up; and (iii) matching resource development plans with overall national development plans. India has worked on this since the First Five Year Plan. Availability of resources is necessary but not enough without changes in technology and institutions: some resource-rich regions are economically backward, and some resource-poor regions are developed. Colonisers exploited colonies' resources through superior technology, so resources contribute to development only with appropriate technology and institutional changes.

concepts.label: Conservation of Resources
concepts.cardText: Irrational consumption and over-utilisation of resources may lead to socio-economic and environmental problems, so resource conservation is important. Gandhiji said, 'There is enough for everybody's need and not for any body's greed.' He saw greedy, selfish individuals and the exploitative nature of modern technology as the root cause of resource depletion, and wanted to replace mass production with production by the masses. The Club of Rome advocated resource conservation systematically in 1968; Schumacher presented Gandhian philosophy in Small is Beautiful (1974); the Brundtland Commission Report (1987) introduced 'Sustainable Development', published as Our Common Future; and the Rio Earth Summit followed in 1992.

concepts.label: Land Resources and Relief
concepts.cardText: Land is a natural resource of utmost importance: it supports natural vegetation, wildlife, human life, economic activities, transport and communication. About 43 per cent of India's land area is plain, providing for agriculture and industry; mountains account for 30 per cent and ensure the perennial flow of some rivers, tourism and ecological benefits; and about 27 per cent is plateau, with rich reserves of minerals, fossil fuels and forests.

concepts.label: Land Use Pattern in India
concepts.cardText: The use of land is determined by physical factors such as topography, climate and soil types, and by human factors such as population density, technological capability, culture and traditions. India's total geographical area is 3.28 million sq km, but land use data is available for only 93 per cent of it. Net sown area varies greatly: over 80 per cent of the total area in Punjab and Haryana, and less than 10 per cent in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Forest area is far lower than the desired 33 per cent of geographical area outlined in the National Forest Policy (1952), considered essential for ecological balance. Continuous use of land without conservation has led to land degradation.

concepts.label: Causes of Land Degradation
concepts.cardText: Ninety-five per cent of our basic needs for food, shelter and clothing come from land. Human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, mining and quarrying have contributed significantly to land degradation. Mining sites are abandoned leaving deep scars; in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha, deforestation due to mining has caused severe degradation. In Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, overgrazing is a main reason. In Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, over irrigation causes water logging, increasing salinity and alkalinity in the soil. Dust from grinding limestone, calcite and soapstone retards infiltration of water into the soil, and industrial effluents pollute land and water.

concepts.label: Soil as a Resource
concepts.cardText: Soil is the most important natural resource: it is the medium of plant growth and supports many living organisms. The soil is a living system; it takes millions of years to form soil up to a few cm in depth. Relief, parent rock or bed rock, climate, vegetation and other forms of life, and time are important factors in soil formation. Forces of nature such as changes in temperature, running water, wind, glaciers and decomposers contribute to it, along with chemical and organic changes. Soil consists of organic (humus) and inorganic materials.

concepts.label: Alluvial Soils
concepts.cardText: Alluvial soil is the most widely spread and important soil. The entire northern plains are made of it, deposited by the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra; it also extends into Rajasthan and Gujarat and is found in the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. It consists of sand, silt and clay, and is coarse near the break of slope, in piedmont plains like Duars, Chos and Terai. By age, it is old alluvial (Bangar), with a higher concentration of kanker nodules, and new alluvial (Khadar), with more fine particles and more fertile. Alluvial soils are very fertile, with potash, phosphoric acid and lime, ideal for sugarcane, paddy and wheat, so these regions are intensively cultivated and densely populated.

concepts.label: Black Soil
concepts.cardText: Black soils are also known as regur soils, and as black cotton soil because they are ideal for growing cotton. Climate and parent rock material are important in their formation. They are typical of the Deccan trap (basalt) region in the northwest Deccan plateau, made up of lava flows, covering the plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh and extending along the Godavari and Krishna valleys. They are made of extremely fine, clayey material, well known for their capacity to hold moisture, and rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime, but poor in phosphoric content. They develop deep cracks in hot weather, which aerate the soil, and are sticky when wet.

concepts.label: Red and Yellow Soils
concepts.cardText: Red soil develops on crystalline igneous rocks in areas of low rainfall in the eastern and southern parts of the Deccan plateau. Yellow and red soils are also found in parts of Odisha, Chhattisgarh, the southern parts of the middle Ganga plain and along the piedmont zone of the Western Ghats. These soils develop a reddish colour due to diffusion of iron in crystalline and metamorphic rocks, and look yellow when they occur in a hydrated form.

concepts.label: Laterite Soil
concepts.cardText: Laterite comes from the Latin word 'later', meaning brick. Laterite soil develops under tropical and subtropical climate with alternate wet and dry seasons, and is the result of intense leaching due to heavy rain. It is mostly deep, acidic (pH below 6.0) and deficient in plant nutrients, found in southern states, the Western Ghats region of Maharashtra, Odisha, parts of West Bengal and the North-east. It is prone to erosion. After soil conservation in the hilly areas of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, it is very useful for growing tea and coffee; red laterite soils in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala suit cashew nut.

concepts.label: Arid Soils
concepts.cardText: Arid soils range from red to brown in colour. They are generally sandy in texture and saline in nature; in some areas the salt content is so high that common salt is obtained by evaporating the water. Due to the dry climate and high temperature, evaporation is faster and the soil lacks humus and moisture. The lower horizons are occupied by Kankar because calcium content increases downwards, and this Kankar layer restricts the infiltration of water. After proper irrigation these soils become cultivable, as in western Rajasthan.

concepts.label: Forest Soils
concepts.cardText: Forest soils are found in hilly and mountainous areas where sufficient rain forests are available. Their texture varies with the mountain environment: loamy and silty on valley sides and coarse grained on the upper slopes. In the snow covered areas of the Himalayas, they experience denudation and are acidic with low humus content. Soils in the lower parts of the valleys, particularly on river terraces and alluvial fans, are fertile.

concepts.label: Soil Erosion
concepts.cardText: The denudation of the soil cover and its subsequent washing down is called soil erosion. Soil formation and erosion go on simultaneously and are usually balanced, but human activities like deforestation, over-grazing, construction and mining disturb the balance, while wind, glaciers and water also cause erosion. Running water cuts deep channels called gullies; the land becomes unfit for cultivation and is called bad land, or ravines in the Chambal basin. When water flows as a sheet down a slope, the top soil is washed away: sheet erosion. Wind blows loose soil off land: wind erosion. Ploughing up and down the slope forms channels for quick flow of water, causing erosion.

concepts.label: Soil Conservation Methods
concepts.cardText: Ploughing along the contour lines slows the flow of water down slopes: contour ploughing. Steps cut on slopes make terraces, and terrace cultivation restricts erosion; the western and central Himalayas have well developed terrace farming. Large fields can be divided into strips with strips of grass left to grow between crops, breaking up the force of the wind: strip cropping. Planting lines of trees to create shelter works in a similar way; these rows are called shelter belts, and they have helped stabilise sand dunes and the desert in western India.
